The team profiled gene expression across the whole genome in diseased cells, watching which genes switch up or down. Numan told von Papen that Eden had merely described the Moscow conference as a great success. Pressed, he denied any request for air bases but admitted Eden had sought Turkey's entry into the war, and he hid behind Turkey's unprepared state. Steinhardt adds that Ankara now feared a preventive Axis move, since the talks could not stay secret. German firms in Turkey, he adds, had been ordered to stop buying Turkish goods and ship out their stocks.

Delivered at Moscow the next day and forwarded to Harriman at Cairo by Navy channels, it answers Harriman's message about preparing the Tehran conference.

Molotov thanks Harriman for his message from Cairo. On the practical questions Harriman had raised, he gives one direction. General Connolly, the American commander in Tehran, may address himself to General Arkadiev. He may do so through the Soviet chargé d'affaires there, about coordinating the measures that interest him. Molotov closes with the hope of meeting soon and sends his most cordial greetings.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d419:
The Declaration on Iran, is dated 1 December 1943. It was signed at Tehran by Churchill, Stalin, and Roosevelt in that order. It is the three powers' formal statement on the country that hosted their conference. An editorial headnote traces the signed original's later path to the State Department.

The three governments recognize the help Iran has given against the common enemy, above all by carrying supplies from overseas to the Soviet Union. They admit the war has caused Iran special economic hardship, and promise such economic help as worldwide shortages of transport and goods allow. After the war, Iran's economic problems will receive full consideration alongside those of other United Nations members. The declaration closes with the three powers at one with Iran's government in desiring the maintenance of her independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, under the Atlantic Charter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d519:
Charles E. Bohlen of the Moscow embassy wrote this second memorandum on December 15, 1943. Bohlen had served as Roosevelt's Russian interpreter at Tehran a fortnight earlier and was one of the State Department's few true Soviet experts. The memorandum appears in the Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Bohlen's memoranda often preserved conversations and judgments that reached print nowhere else, because he was present where other Americans were not. A paper from mid-December belongs to the stocktaking after the summit, when officials wrote down what the new relationship with Moscow seemed to mean. Readers get a young diplomat's careful record, made before hindsight could tidy it.
frus-1944-quebec-d19:
Churchill sent another message to President Roosevelt on August 5, 1944. It came a day after his previous message. The State Department printed both letters. They sit in the pre-conference correspondence of the Quebec 1944 volume.

The first week of August 1944 moved faster than any plan. American armor was racing across France. The Red Army stood before Warsaw. Churchill wrote daily because the map changed daily. For readers, a second message in two days shows something clear. The Prime Minister was working hard to keep diplomacy level. He tried to match events that his own strategy had helped unleash.
frus-1944-quebec-d119:
Winston Churchill sent this personal, top-secret telegram, numbered 779, to President Roosevelt on September 4, 1944. Britain's War Cabinet was deeply disturbed by events in Warsaw. Stalin had refused to let Allied aircraft use Soviet airfields to supply the Polish fighters, and Churchill feared the wider damage to relations with Russia.

Churchill begged Roosevelt to let American aircraft drop supplies and land on Russian airfields without formal Soviet consent. The Russians, he argued, could hardly reject a finished act and might even welcome it. Britain would share full responsibility. He also warned that Warsaw's fall would destroy Premier Mikołajczyk's standing and his talks with the Lublin Committee.
frus-1944-quebec-d219:
An editors' note closes the zones story at Quebec. The Combined Chiefs' memorandum of September 16, 1944, was agreed by Roosevelt and Churchill later that day and folded into the final summary of conference conclusions as paragraphs 33 and 34. A map reflecting the decisions was prepared in Washington immediately afterward and sent to Ambassador Winant on September 21.

The note also marks what Quebec did not settle. The allocation of sectors inside Berlin had been left open by the London protocol of September 12, and no evidence has been found that the question was discussed at Quebec at all. Further Anglo-American negotiations led to the tripartite agreement signed in the European Advisory Commission on November 14, 1944.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d19: A week after winning a fourth term, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on 14 November 1944. The directive goes to the supreme commander of the Allied forces in Europe. It covers the first weeks after fighting stops, before the three powers agree on a joint paper. The War and State Departments wrote it, and the Treasury agreed to it. A joint civil affairs board had not yet cleared it. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d219:

Harriman expects the subject to come up at the coming meeting. His views run as follows. It serves the United States to help the Soviet economy grow. The Russians should be given to understand that such help hangs on their conduct in world affairs. And talk of long-term credits should be kept wholly apart from the running Lend-Lease negotiations. Joshua, the sixth book of the Bible in King James translation, begins after the death of Moses. Joshua takes command of the Israelites and leads them across into Canaan, the land they believed had been promised to them. Battles, alliances, and the settling of territory fill most of its chapters.

Readers find the fall of Jericho, the division of land among the twelve tribes, and cities set aside for refuge and for the Levites. Near the end Joshua gathers the people, recalls what God has done, and charges them to stay faithful. The book works both as a conquest account and as a record of a covenant people taking shape.

Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, amid England's civil war, and founded modern political philosophy on fear and contract rather than divine right. Without a sovereign, he argues, human life in the state of nature is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. War of every man against every man is his diagnosis.

The cure is surrender: subjects covenant to obey an absolute power, the Leviathan, in exchange for security. Hobbes builds the case with geometrical confidence through human nature, language, religion, and the church's proper subordination. Readers may reject his remedy, but his question, what justifies obedience, still organizes political argument.
tob-9219:
Around the year 140, a Roman Christian known as Hermas recorded a series of strange visions. His work, the Shepherd of Hermas, appears here in William Wake's translation, in a set of early Christian writings once left outside the New Testament. Some early churches read it almost as Scripture.

Hermas sees a tower being built from living stones, a picture of the church, and meets a shepherd who gives him strict commands. The great question is whether Christians who sin after baptism can be forgiven, and how. The visions answer with both warning and hope, and they show a young church working out its rules.
tob-0019:
Peter leads a tour of the world to come in the Apocalypse of Peter, one of the earliest Christian visions of the afterlife. This entry rests on a verified pre-1930 public-domain edition. Some early churches read the work nearly as Scripture before later ages set it aside.

Heaven shows its brightness, and hell shows punishments fitted closely to each sin: liars, murderers, and the cruel each meet a matching torment. Later ages borrowed the pattern freely, down to the great infernos of medieval poetry. The vision is stern, vivid, and oddly hopeful, since mercy keeps breaking in. Few short texts cast so long a shadow.

Laurence Dermott wrote the Ahiman Rezon for the Antient Grand Lodge, the rowdy rival of Anderson's Masons. First issued in the 1750s, his constitution defends older customs against what he saw as modern tampering. Waite's scholars and traditionalists alike still argue over its claims.

Dermott writes with wit and earthiness where Anderson is stately. Charges, rules, and songs fill the book, along with sharp words for the other side. The schism between Antients and Moderns shaped Masonry for sixty years. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, this abridged copy gives the other founding text of English Freemasonry, the one with jokes.
tob-4219:
Jan van Ruysbroeck, prior of Groenendaal near Brussels, wrote the three works gathered here in the fourteenth century. The Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage maps the soul's active, inward, and God-seeing lives. The Sparkling Stone and the Book of Supreme Truth press further, into union without difference.

The 1916 English volume puts his masterworks between one set of covers. Ruysbroeck writes in images of fountains, bees, and summer valleys, then suddenly in hard paradox. Contemporaries called him the Ecstatic Doctor. Verified from the 1919 edition, the triple volume gives the Flemish mystic whole, at the height of his strange and beautiful powers.
tob-4319:
Meister Eckhart, the German Dominican of about 1260 to 1328, preached sermons that still startle. C. de B. Evans translated them in a modern version of 1924, and volume one gathers sermons and treatises on the Godhead beyond God. The church condemned some of his claims after his death.

Eckhart teaches detachment so complete that the soul lets go even of God as an idea, and speaks of the Word being born in the soul as in Bethlehem. Paradox is his native tongue. Verified from the 1919 edition record, Evans's first volume gives medieval mysticism's boldest voice in English built for modern ears.
fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-3-microcosmi-1:
The second tome of Fludd's history, from 1619, turns to the microcosm: man himself. Its long Latin title lists the supernatural, natural, and contrary sides of man's story. Fludd was a London doctor with a cosmic reach.

He traces the soul's fall, its powers, and its life in the body. Health and sickness get read as signs of inner order. Spirits and stars act on man in his scheme. The text is dense and diagram-rich in spirit. It forms the core of his claim that man sums up the whole world.
fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-4-microcosmi-s:
This 1619 section of Fludd's second tome treats the technical side of the microcosm. Its Latin title names it De Technica Microcosmi Historia. Fludd turns from man's soul to the arts man practices.

He covers skills from number and measure to war and craft. Each art is set inside his mirror scheme of world and man. The learning is wide, if the system strains at times. Engraved figures in the full edition aid the text. The section closes his survey of human art, and shows a Renaissance mind at full stretch.
shackleton-south-1919:
Ernest Shackleton published South in 1919, the story of his last great expedition of 1914 to 1917. His ship Endurance sailed to cross Antarctica from sea to sea. Instead, the ice caught the ship, crushed it, and sank it, leaving 28 men on the floes.

Shackleton tells how the crew camped on drifting ice for months, then sailed lifeboats to Elephant Island. From there he made the famous open-boat run to South Georgia and crossed its peaks to find help. Every man lived. The book is the leader's own record of endurance and command.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-19:
Volume nineteen of Rodkinson's set steps outside the Talmud text itself: it is the first volume of his History of the Talmud. Rodkinson, a Russian-born scholar who settled in America, wrote the history to frame his twenty-volume translation. The 1918 edition gathers his long study of the work's making.

He traces the oral law from Moses through the Mishnah's writing under Rabbi Judah the Prince. Then he follows the centuries of debate in Babylon that grew into the Gemara. Lives of the great rabbis and schools fill the story. Readers who finish the translation here learn how the vast book itself came to be.
crowley-equinox-vol-3-no-1-1919:
The Blue Equinox broke the journal's silence in March 1919, as volume three, number one. Crowley recast The Equinox as the public charter of the O T O, his second order. The blue covers held a manifesto, not just a miscellany.

Its core is the Gnostic Mass, the central rite of the O T O, printed for all to read. The constitutions of the order and the word of the Law of Thelema stand beside it. The issue told the world what the order was and what it claimed. It is the most famed single number of the whole journal.
fort-book-of-the-damned-1919:
Charles Fort spent years in newspaper files clipping wonders, and his first harvest came out in 1919. The Book of the Damned gathers rains of fish, falls of stones, strange lights, and folk who vanish. Fort calls such things damned because science shuts them out of its world.

His method is the pile: case on case, each clipped and cited, until doubt itself looks thin. His prose mocks the priests of science in a voice like no other writer's. The book founded the study of the strange that now bears his name, Forteana. It taught the world a new way to doubt its teachers.
dunsany-tales-of-three-hemispheres-1919:
A phrase that named a whole kind of story was born in Dunsany's book of 1919. Tales of Three Hemispheres gives us beyond the fields we know, the gate phrase of portal fantasy. Its tales cross from our world to lands that run on dream's laws.

Old gods walk in new cities, and travelers trade the known fields for stranger ground. The book mixes his myth tales with yarns of a more modern cut. That mix shows Dunsany at a turn in his long career. The phrase alone would earn the volume its place in letters.
cabell-jurgen-1919:
James Branch Cabell sent a pawnbroker through myth in Jurgen, his comic novel of 1919. Jurgen wins back his youth and roams through hell, heaven, and old tales. He meets queens, gods, and his own past loves. Wit is his sword and shield.

Courts charged the book with lewd acts, and the case made it famed. The ban drew crowds of new fans. Back of the jokes lies a sad view of love and age. The book made sly, learned fun a mark of high class tale craft. Jurgen claims he seeks fair play, yet takes each boon life grants. That gap twixt word and deed is the joke at the book's heart.
merritt-moon-pool-1919:
Lost realms and a bright dweller call to men in Abraham Merritt's novel The Moon Pool, from 1919. A team of bold men finds old ruins in the south seas. A gate of moon light leads down to a vast cave world of strange life and old gods.

Peril and awe mix in rich, lush prose. Merritt piles wonder on wonder at pulp speed. The book helped set the mold for lost-world tales in the United States. Its glow shaped hosts of pulp tales that came in its wake. A bright being in the pool can heal or kill with its touch. Its gifts draw greed, faith, and war from all who meet it.
doyle-vital-message-1919:
Arthur Conan Doyle presses his cause in The Vital Message, his next book of 1919. The Great War had left a land full of grief. Doyle holds that word from the dead is not a fad, but the most grave news of the age. He sums the proof, meets the foes, and calls the church to take the new light to heart with speed.

His tone is that of a man on a quest, not a sage at rest. The book is his flag in the post war push of the faith. It shows his zeal at full heat.
burchard-corrector-decretum-19:
Burchard of Worms asks the flock hard asks in the Corrector, Book 19 of his Decretum, writ near 1012. Burchard was a bishop who built a vast book of church law. This book is a quiz for priests to put to folk who own their sins. Have you flown by night with Diana? Have you feasted with souls, or wrought harm by charms in the dark?

Each sin gets its price in fasts and prayer. The text shows what folk of that age held true in their hearts. It holds the famed canon Episcopi in full. Sages mine it still.
routledge-mystery-easter-island-1919:
Katherine Routledge led the Mana trip to Easter Island in 1914. Her book The Mystery of Easter Island came out in 1919. The trip made the first full study of the isle and its great stone heads, the moai. Routledge writes as both sailor and field worker.

She tells how the heads were cut, moved, and raised, and what the isle folk said of them. Strange carved birds, caves, and old rites fill the tale. The ship's tale frames the work: storms, waits, and war news from far off. The book stands as the base study of the isle.
augustine-confessions-watts-vol-1-1919:
William Watts gave Augustine's Confessions English dress in 1631. A 1919 print of that old dress fills this book. Book One holds Books One to Eight of the Confessions. Augustine was a north African bishop and a great mind of the Church.

A wild youth, a trade in fine speech, and a flight from his mother's faith fill the tale. The famed scene in the garden at Milan turns his life at last. Watts's dress keeps the tang of the age of King James. The book is the first great tale of a soul in the West.
defoe-robinson-crusoe-1719:
Daniel Defoe published Robinson Crusoe in 1719, often called the first English novel in the modern sense. The book invented realist fiction, the castaway narrative, and the economic individual as hero for readers. Defoe wrote it at sixty, drawing on castaway tales like that of Alexander Selkirk in print.

Crusoe, a York sailor, is wrecked alone on an island near the Orinoco's mouth for years. He builds, plants, pots, and keeps a journal, turning despair into methodical daily work and prayer. A footprint in the sand terrifies him, then brings him Friday, his companion and convert in time. Rescue, mutineers, and a return to England close a tale of self-reliance and providence in balance. Its plain style and concrete detail made fiction feel true to common life.
hesse-demian-1919:
Hermann Hesse published Demian in 1919, his novel of awakening, first issued under the name Emil Sinclair. Emil Sinclair's journey from bourgeois innocence to selfhood under Demian's spell made the book the voice of German youth. Hesse, broken by war and analysis, wrote it in three weeks of 1917 as a confession.

Sinclair, a schoolboy, is blackmailed by Kromer over a lie and rescued by the uncanny Max Demian. Demian teaches him to read Cain's mark as a sign of the elect, not a brand of shame. War takes both to the front, where Demian dies, promising to live on inside the friend he shaped. Abraxas, the god who is both good and evil, names the wholeness Sinclair must grow toward in Hesse's creed of selfhood. The novel's influence on young readers, from 1919 to the counterculture, is hard to overstate.
vega-fuenteovejuna-1619:
Lope de Vega wrote Fuenteovejuna around 1619, a Spanish play based on a true revolt from the 1400s. A cruel commander abuses the people of the village of Fuenteovejuna. He seizes women and rules by fear. The villagers at last rise together and kill him.

Royal judges arrive to find who struck the blows. Under torture, old and young give one answer: Fuenteovejuna did it. The king must pardon the whole town or punish it as one. The play praises unity and justice against tyranny. Its famous reply has become a lasting symbol of a people standing together.
anderson-winesburg-ohio-1919:
Sherwood Anderson published Winesburg, Ohio in 1919, a set of linked short stories about a small town. Young George Willard, a newspaper reporter, listens as townspeople confess their private truths. Anderson calls them grotesques: people warped by clinging to one truth alone. A teacher, a doctor, a farmer, and others take their turn.

Each tale is short, plain, and quietly sad. At night the streets of Winesburg fill with loneliness and unspoken longing. George at last leaves for the city, carrying all he has heard. The book helped shape the modern American short story. Its method of linked tales has been copied many times since.
keynes-economic-consequences-1919:
John Maynard Keynes served as a British Treasury adviser at the Paris peace talks after the First World War and resigned in protest. His 1919 book The Economic Consequences of the Peace tells why. It made him famous almost at once on both sides of the Atlantic.

Keynes argues that the treaty terms, above all the huge payments demanded of Germany, would wreck trade and breed fresh conflict. He draws sharp portraits of the leaders at Paris and weighs their choices coldly. His warning read like prophecy within a generation, as Europe slid toward a second war.
aurobindo-human-cycle-1919:
Sri Aurobindo wrote The Human Cycle as essays in his journal Arya during the First World War, and the book appeared in 1919. Aurobindo had been a revolutionary against British rule in India before turning to yoga and philosophy. Here he offers a philosophy of history on the grand scale.

He traces societies through stages ruled in turn by symbol, custom, reason, and self-seeking trade. Beyond those stages he foresees a spiritual age, in which human unity grows from inner change rather than from force. The book states the hopeful core of Aurobindo's later teaching on the evolution of society.
wilson-complete-dictionary-of-astrology-:
James Wilson was a London astrologer whose Complete Dictionary of Astrology appeared in 1819. The book defines the terms of the art from aspect to zodiac in alphabetical order. It became the reference work of the early astrological revival.

Wilson explains each term plainly, often with a working example drawn from a real chart or a past master. He is frank about where authors disagree, letting the reader see the art's unsettled corners. Practitioners kept the dictionary at hand because no English book had gathered the vocabulary in one place before. It assumes a reader with a chart in hand and a question to answer.
beaumont-fletcher-maids-tragedy-1619:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher were the most popular English playwrights of their generation, writing just after Shakespeare. Their tragedy The Maid's Tragedy was performed by the King's Men around 1610. It was first printed in 1619.

The plot turns on a wedding night secret. The king has forced the bride, Evadne, to remain his mistress, and her new husband learns the truth too late. Shame, loyalty, and revenge drive the court toward murder. The play's dark picture of a corrupt king made it the defining tragedy of court corruption in its era, and actors revived it often.
shelley-cenci-1819:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote The Cenci in Italy in 1819, basing it on a true Roman story from 1599. Shelley hoped the play could be staged in London, but its subject made that impossible in his lifetime. He modeled its plain, forceful style on Jacobean tragedy.

Count Francesco Cenci is a monster of cruelty who rejoices in tormenting his family. His daughter Beatrice, driven past endurance, arranges his murder with her mother and brother. The law then punishes the victims more harshly than it ever punished the tyrant. Shelley explores how violence corrupts even the innocent. The play is his most stage-worthy drama.
woolf-night-and-day-1919:
Virginia Woolf published Night and Day in 1919, her second novel. Woolf wrote it in a more traditional shape than her later books, with a full plot and clear chapters. Readers sometimes use it to see where her famous experimental style began.

Katharine Hilbery, granddaughter of a famous poet, spends her days helping with his biography and her nights secretly studying mathematics. She becomes engaged to the earnest William Rodney, then finds herself drawn to the less polished Ralph Denham. A second couple, Mary Datchet and her suffrage work, mirrors the main story. Woolf quietly questions marriage, family fame, and women's work. The comedy is gentle and the intelligence constant.
sinclair-brass-check-1919:
Upton Sinclair published The Brass Check in 1919, at his own expense, after no commercial house would take it. Sinclair had spent twenty years fighting editors who trimmed his socialism, and this book names names. Its title comes from the brass checks men once bought in brothels, his metaphor for bought journalism.

The book documents, case by case, how American newspapers served their owners and advertisers: suppressed stories, planted lies, and crusades steered by business interests. Sinclair draws on his own clashes with the press over The Jungle and his later campaigns. He proposes reforms, from public ownership to reader-funded papers. The Brass Check is the first systematic American critique of the press, and its charges still start arguments.
irving-sketch-book-1819:
Washington Irving published The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon in 1819, writing under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon. Irving was an American author living in England, and his sketches move between the two countries. Two tales in the volume soon became famous across the English-speaking world.

One tale sends Rip Van Winkle to sleep in the Catskill hills for twenty years. Another follows schoolmaster Ichabod Crane on his night ride past the Headless Horseman. Gentle essays on English country life and Christmas customs fill out the rest of the book. The Sketch Book proved that an American writer could win a wide audience at home and abroad.
chekhov-bishop-1919:
Constance Garnett's 1919 Chekhov volume takes its name from The Bishop, one of his last and finest stories. Bishop Pyotr, ill during Holy Week, feels the weight of office, ceremony, and distance from simple faith. Only his mother's visit brings him close to his younger, freer self.

The Letter turns on a message carried between an exiled bishop's circle and a proud dean. Easter Eve sets a monk's grief and joy against the river and fireworks of the feast night. Chekhov wrote these tales near the end of his life, and their tone is quiet and grave. The volume shows his late mastery at its most tender.
hoffmann-serapion-brethren-vol1-1819:
The Serapion Brethren is E. T. A. Hoffmann's great cycle of tales, first published in German from 1819. Alexander Ewing translated volume one into English in 1886. A circle of friends meets to tell stories, debate them, and judge each tale by the vivid sight of its teller.

Inside the frame, tales of artists, madmen, automata, and ghosts unfold in turn. The Nutcracker story and tales of the singer Antonia are among the treasures here. Hoffmann blends music, dream, and terror with a craftsman's care. The frame talks give the book a second pleasure: friends arguing over what makes a story true. Volume one sets the pattern for the whole cycle.
hoffmann-serapion-brethren-vol2-1819:
Volume two of The Serapion Brethren completes Hoffmann's story cycle in Alexander Ewing's English, issued in 1892. The friends of the frame meet again, and the tales grow stranger as the evenings pass. Singers, goldsmiths, doubles, and haunted houses take their turns in the talk.

Hoffmann saves some of his richest inventions for these later nights. Music keeps its central place, as both bliss and curse for those who serve it. The arguments between tales sharpen, too, testing fancy against fact. Ewing's two volumes together give English readers the full cycle. The work remains the model for the nineteenth-century tale collection, frame and all.
kalila-wa-dimna-knatchbull-1819:
Wyndham Knatchbull translated Kalila and Dimna into English at Oxford in 1819, the first English rendering from the Arabic. The book, also called The Fables of Bidpai, tells animal tales inside a frame of a king and his philosopher. Lions, jackals, doves, and apes act out the rules of power, friendship, and caution.

The tales began in India's Panchatantra, passed into Persian, then into Arabic in the eighth century. From Arabic they spread across Europe and fed its beast fable for a thousand years. Kalila and Dimna, the two jackals of the first book, give the whole its name. Knatchbull's version marks the Arabic stage of that long westward road. The stories taught statecraft through animals.
agnostus-epitimia-1619:
Irenäus Agnostus published Epitimia Fr R C in German in 1619. The subtitle promises a final revelation, or disclosure, about the Fraternity of the Rose Cross. Agnostus wrote near the end of the pamphlet cycle that had burned through German print since the manifestos appeared.

The work claims to lay the brotherhood open at last, after years of claim and counterclaim. It closes the run of replies that stretched from 1617 to 1619. Whether its disclosure settles anything is for the reader to judge from the text itself. As a document, it marks the point where the first great Rose Cross debate burned itself out.
luxemburg-junius-pamphlet-1919:
Luxemburg wrote her Junius Pamphlet in a Berlin prison cell in 1916. The Socialist Publication Society issued it in English in 1919 as The Crisis in the German Social-Democracy. Germany's Social Democrats had voted war credits in 1914, backing their own government's war. Luxemburg, writing under the name Junius, indicts that choice.

She calls the war an imperialist slaughter and the party's vote a betrayal. The pamphlet looks to a rebuilt international movement of workers against war. Its pages burn with grief for the party she helped build. The text stands as a founding voice of revolutionary anti war socialism. Few prison writings carry such weight.
faria-cause-sommeil-lucide-1819:
The Abbe Faria stated the suggestion theory in De la cause du sommeil lucide, printed in French in 1819. Lucid sleep, his name for the mesmeric trance, needs no magnetic fluid, he argues. The subject's own concentration raises the state. The operator's command guides it, but the power sits in the sleeper.

Faria had learned his method in India and tested it on Paris stages. His book studies the nature of man through this one strange door. Braid himself later cited Faria as a forerunner of true hypnosis. The French original is a precursor text of the whole field. It shifts the wonder from fluid to mind. Modern suggestion theory starts on its pages.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol19:
Volume XIX of the Journal of Discourses came from Liverpool in 1878, the first volume printed after Brigham Young's death. His sermons still appear, drawn from the record, alongside talks by the leaders who followed him. The Twelve Apostles now carry the church, and their voices grow stronger in the set.

The transition shows in the preaching: old doctrines restated by new mouths, counsel fitted to fresh troubles. The Journal kept its form through the change, shorthand to print as before. Volume XIX lets readers watch a movement pass its first great succession without breaking stride.
waley-li-po-1919:
Li Po drank, wandered, and wrote the freest verse of Tang China, and Arthur Waley's The Poet Li Po of 1919 gave him to English readers. The study joins a biography of Li Bai, who lived from 701 to 762, with thirty translated poems. Waley drew on Chinese sources to build the first substantial English account of the poet.

Mountains, rivers, moonlight, and partings fill the poems, rendered in Waley's clear, quiet English. The life matches the verse: court favor, exile, and endless roads. Readers meet here the poet China itself ranks among its greatest, in the version that first carried his name west.
cid-lay-rose-bacon-1919:
Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, the Cid, rides through Spain's oldest surviving epic, The Lay of the Cid, from about 1200. R. Selden Rose and Leonard Bacon rendered it in English verse in 1919. Exiled by his king, the Cid wins land, wealth, and honor by his sword, and takes Valencia as his prize.

The poem honors loyalty under insult: its hero serves the king who wronged him, and shames the coward sons-in-law who wrong his daughters. Its spare, direct style feels closer to history than to romance. Rose and Bacon's translation carried the national epic of Spain to English readers in ringing form.
antar-hamilton-1819:
Terrick Hamilton Englished the romance of Antar in 1819 and 1820, the first version in the language, complete in four volumes gathered here as one text. Antar ibn Shaddad, the black knight-poet of pre-Islamic Arabia, fights, loves, and sings his way through the vast Sirah that bears his name. Born to a slave mother, he wins freedom and fame by spear and verse.

The folk epic ranks among the longest in world literature, swelling over centuries of storytelling. Duels, raids, and the beloved Abla fill its sprawling, splendid course. Hamilton's rendering introduced English readers to a hero the Arab world had cherished for a thousand years.
conrad-arrow-of-gold-1919:
The Arrow of Gold, published in 1919, is Conrad's late romance of Marseilles in the 1870s. A young seaman, Blunt, is drawn into gun-running for the Carlist pretender to Spain's throne, and into the orbit of the mysterious Dona Rita.

Rita, an heiress of strange beauty and a wilder past, is fought over by smugglers, artists, and aristocrats. Conrad tells the tale at one remove, through an older man's memory, giving it a haze of legend. The novel divides readers: some find it tired, others a dreamlike farewell to his world of conspiracy and desire.
kafka-in-der-strafkolonie-1919:
In der Strafkolonie, published in 1919, is Kafka's story of a penal colony and its execution machine. An officer demonstrates the apparatus to a visiting traveler: it kills by slowly writing the condemned man's sentence into his flesh with needles.

The officer believes in the machine and its dead inventor with religious faith. The traveler watches, unwilling either to approve or to intervene. When the machine is set to judge the officer himself, it fails in a spasm of self-destruction. Kafka wrote the story in 1914, as Europe entered its own machinery of death. Its horror is quiet, procedural, and complete.
russell-intro-mathematical-philosophy-19:
Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy, published in 1919, is Russell's plain-language account of the ideas behind Principia Mathematica. He wrote much of it in Brixton prison, where he was held for an anti-war article, working without a library.

Russell explains number, infinity, series, and the theory of descriptions for readers with no training in symbols. The paradox that shook the foundations of logic gets a clear, almost cheerful hearing. His aim was to show that the great work's ideas could live outside its notation. The book remains the friendliest door into mathematical logic ever written by one of its makers.
whitehead-principles-natural-knowledge-1:
An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Natural Knowledge, published in 1919, is Whitehead's first book in the philosophy of nature. After Principia Mathematica he turned to physics itself, asking how science builds its world of points, instants, and particles.

His method of extensive abstraction derives those ideal entities from what we actually perceive: durations, events, and their overlaps. The aim is to found physics on experience without fictions. The book is technical and demanding, the start of Whitehead's long second career in philosophy. Readers of his later metaphysics will find its roots here, in the problem of how nature is known.
royce-lectures-modern-idealism-1919:
Lectures on Modern Idealism, published in 1919, three years after Royce's death, prints the last lecture course he built on the idealist tradition. Kant, Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel are his subjects, the four Germans who made modern idealism.

Royce treats each thinker as a stage in one argument about selfhood and the absolute. His sympathy is with Hegel, but his exposition stays fair to all four, in the clear style of a practiced lecturer. The course sums up the tradition he had spent his life extending. It is his last word on idealism, and a graceful one.
laski-authority-state-1919:
Authority in the Modern State, published in 1919, is Harold J. Laski's pluralist attack on state sovereignty, drawn from his early Harvard years. Against the doctrine that the state commands all loyalty, Laski argues that authority is in fact dispersed among groups.

Churches, unions, and associations hold real allegiance, and the state's claim to stand above them is a fiction that experience refutes. Federalism of function, not territory, is his model. The book is learned in the history of political thought and brisk in its conclusions. It made Laski's name and set the pluralist program he later revised but never abandoned.
plos-pone-0003419:
László Pecze and co-authors studied how skin cells react to chili compounds in this 2008 paper. Capsaicin, the heat in chili peppers, can also dull pain. A stronger cousin, resiniferatoxin, opens a channel called TRPV1 for good. That flood of calcium can remove pain-sensing nerve cells.

Oddly, the main cells of the skin did not react the same way. These cells, called keratinocytes, proved resistant to both compounds. Their toughness sets them apart from the nerves around them. Drug makers must weigh that split when designing skin-applied pain treatments. Nerves and skin, though close neighbors, answer these compounds in opposite ways.
plos-pone-0003519:
Elina Salmela and co-authors mapped population structure in northern Europe in this 2008 study. Genome-wide data can reveal fine patterns of human variation. The team analyzed almost 250,000 DNA markers per person. Samples numbered 945, from Finland, Sweden, northern Germany, and Great Britain.

Even within northern Europe, clear genetic clusters appeared. Eastern and western Finland differed, as history would suggest. Geography and past migration carved structure into the genome. Such maps matter when gene studies compare cases and controls. Such maps also serve as base lines for gene hunts in each region. Finnish groups proved especially rich in fine detail.
plos-pone-0003619:
Pascal F. Egea and co-authors solved a docking protein's structure in this 2008 paper. All cells use a signal recognition particle to guide new proteins to membranes. Its receptor catches those proteins at the membrane for secretion or insertion. The team worked with the receptor from Pyrococcus furiosus, a heat-loving archaeon.

They present the first X-ray structures of an archaeal FtsY receptor. The shapes clarify the targeting step at the membrane. A system conserved across all life can be read in this ancient version. Such structures anchor models of protein delivery.
plos-pone-0003719:
Gaoping Xiao, Eirik W. Lundblad, Mina Izadjoo, and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2008. External guide sequences are short RNAs that steer an enzyme to cut a chosen target RNA. That trick can shut a gene off after it is read. The team aimed it at a dangerous bacterium's control gene.

They used the method in E. coli to block MglB, a virulence regulator of Francisella tularensis, the tularemia germ. Blocking the regulator shows the switch can be reached and silenced. The approach offers a programmable off-switch for probing how dangerous pathogens run their genes.
plos-pone-0003819:
Cyril Touboul, Wassim Badiou, Julien Saada, and colleagues published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Heavy bleeding after childbirth can kill a new mother within hours. Selective arterial embolisation blocks the bleeding arteries from inside, using imaging to guide the block. The team assessed how well it works at scale.

They studied 102 patients with life-threatening post-partum haemorrhage who underwent the procedure. The results measure the technique's efficacy and help pin down its best indications. Knowing when embolisation works best guides emergency teams facing one of childbirth's deadliest complications.
plos-pone-0003919:
Leigh Anne Eller, Michael A. Eller, Benson Ouma, and co-authors set lab reference ranges in Uganda in 2008. Vaccine trials now run in many countries at once. Each site needs local ranges for normal lab values to judge safety. Values from other populations can mislabel healthy local volunteers.

Their PLOS ONE article reports ranges from healthy adult blood donors in Uganda. Those ranges show where local norms depart from imported ones. Using them keeps trials from excluding healthy people by mistake. It also sharpens safety checks while new vaccines are tested in the region. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004019:
Michael W. Miller, Heather M. Swanson, Lisa L. Wolfe, and co-authors assessed prion disease in deer in 2008. Chronic wasting disease spreads through deer family populations. Scrapie does the same in sheep flocks. Such epidemics seem able to threaten whole host populations.

Their PLOS ONE article weighs the ecological fallout in natural settings. Mountain lions prey on deer and may shape the epidemic. Predators could remove sick deer faster than healthy ones. The study asks whether prions, predators, and deer together decide population fate. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004119:
Mansour Aliabadian, Mohammad Kaboli, Vincent Nijman, and co-authors tested DNA barcoding in birds in 2009. Barcoding uses the COI gene to identify species by DNA. It has worked across many animal groups. Closely allied neighboring species, though, sometimes blur together.

Their PLOS ONE article tests distance-based barcoding across three genes. The target was delimiting parapatric species, neighbors with touching ranges. Performance varied in how cleanly the genes split those species. The study warns barcoding needs backup where bird ranges meet. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004219:
Shota Nakamura and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The SARS epidemic of 2003 and fears of bird flu pandemics showed the need for surveillance systems that catch new infectious diseases early. The team applied next-generation parallel sequencing, a high-throughput way to read DNA, directly to clinical samples.

Their unbiased approach reads whatever genetic material is present in nasal and fecal specimens, without first choosing which virus to look for. That direct metagenomic detection can name viral pathogens in a single run. The method points toward outbreak watch systems that do not need to guess the culprit in advance.
plos-pone-0004319:
Françoise Gondois-Rey and colleagues published this hepatitis C study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells produce type I interferon during viral infection. Interferon alpha therapy clears hepatitis C virus in more than half of chronic patients. That success suggests the patients' own interferon production may be impaired.

The team compared how these cells respond to hepatitis C virus versus influenza and human herpesvirus type-1. They report that HCV is a weak inducer of interferon alpha in these cells. A virus that barely trips the alarm can explain how HCV settles in for decades.
plos-pone-0004419: In 2009, Warter, Cohen, and Benureau found viral teamwork. Nontranslated RNA sequences and NS5A protein cooperatively boosted GB virus B fitness. The RNA-protein handshake mattered in living hosts. The finding informs hepatitis C models. The surrogate virus proved highly valuable.
plos-pone-0004519: In 2009, Ruas, Bernardes, and Ferm found a missing sugar-binder tilting immunity. Lack of galectin-3 drove the response to the fungus toward Th2. The absent lectin skewed immune defenses. The finding maps fungal immunity balance. The fungus causes a chronic lung disease.
plos-pone-0004619: In 2009, Fontana, Cestaro, and Velasco built a faster genome labeler anew. Rapid annotation of anonymous genome sequences used semantic similarities and weighting. The tool predicted gene functions well. The method aids sequencing projects today. The auto labeling is quick and cheap.
plos-pone-0004719: In 2009, Michelsen, Thomas, and Taylor found IBD gene variants boosting a gut protein. IBD-associated TL1A haplotypes raised TL1A protein expression. The variants cranked up the signal hard. The study maps inflammatory bowel disease genetics. The gut protein boosts IFN-γ.
massinger-fatal-dowry-1619:
Philip Massinger and Nathan Field wrote The Fatal Dowry, a Jacobean tragedy first staged around 1619. A young officer comes home from war to find his dead father's body held by creditors who will not release it for burial. To settle the shame, he marries into a rich and corrupt household.

The marriage quickly turns sour, and claims of betrayal push the hero toward a fierce defense of his honor. Murder and revenge follow, handled in the sharp, formal verse of the early Stuart stage. Readers meet a world where debt, pride, and loose morals drive men to ruin. The play still ranks among the strongest revenge dramas of its time.
drayton-idea-1619:
Michael Drayton shaped his sonnet sequence Idea over some twenty-five years, and the final form appeared in 1619. The sixty-three sonnets address a beloved he calls Idea, linked in his life to Anne Goodyer. She is both a real woman and a figure for beauty itself in the poems.

The opening sonnets compare the poet to a sailor reporting a long and risky voyage. Later poems play with conceits about murder, counting griefs, and a heart that will not rest. Standing beside Sidney and Spenser, the sequence shows an Elizabethan poet polishing the same love poems across a whole working life.
blok-iambs-1919:
Alexander Blok gathered poems in iambic meter under the plain title Iambs, printed in Russian in 1919. He was Russia's leading Symbolist poet, famed for The Twelve and his verses to a beautiful lady. These late poems were shaped in the heat and fear of revolt.

Blok turns the steady beat of the iamb toward Russia's fate and the artist's place in a burning world. The tone is tense, grieving, and musical at once. Gone is the dreamy haze of his youth. In its place stands a poet speaking plainly while his old world collapses fast around him, line by ringing line, year by bitter year.
gems-of-chinese-verse-1919:
Tang dynasty verse fills Gems of Chinese Verse, Englished by W. J. B. Fletcher in 1919. Du Fu and Li Bai stand among its poets, the twin peaks of China's golden age. Moonlit rivers, frontier posts, and dawn farewells supply its scenes.

Fletcher, an early English voice for Chinese poetry, prized clarity and music in his versions. Brief lyrics carry vast feeling in a few exact images. Soldiers, exiles, wives, and wanderers all speak in turn. The anthology gives new readers a fine first path into a refined art, one that shaped verse across East Asia for a thousand years and more.
andreae-turris-babel-1619:
Johann Valentin Andreae survey the chaos around the Rosy Cross in Turris Babel, written in Latin in 1619. Andreae, likely an author of the Rosicrucian manifestos himself, watches Europe argue over his own creation. Judgments clash like tongues at Babel, and he records the confusion with dry, insider irony.

Pamphlets for and against the unseen brotherhood had flooded the presses for years. Andreae sorts the praise, panic, and mockery with a cool hand. The book forms a key record of the Rosicrucian furor at its height. Few documents show a craze so well from inside, by a man who helped start it.
berzelius-essai-proportions-chimiques-18:
Berzelius sets out his essay on chemical proportions in French in 1819, laying ground for the modern table of atomic weights. He fixed the relative weights of the elements with new care. His letter symbols for the elements, H, O, and the rest, are the ones chemists still write today.

Measurement replaces recipe as the soul of chemistry in his hands. Long tables of trials back each number he dares to print. The work turned a craft of mixtures into a science of exact amounts. Few books did more to give chemistry its modern shape, and students still use his symbols daily without knowing his name.
faria-sommeil-lucide-1819:
Abbe Faria explains lucid sleep without magnets in his treatise, Tome One, in French from 1819. Trance, he argues, springs from the subject's own mind, not from any fluid. The Goan priest, working in Paris, showed that expectation and a firm voice could induce the sleep he studied in his pupils.

His theory of suggestion came decades before the word grew famous. Braid later owned Faria as a forerunner of his own work on hypnotism. The book was cut short by its author's early death in Paris. It marks the birth of psychological hypnotism, the moment the marvel moved from the magnetizer's hands into the sleeper's mind.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-19:
Open war reaches the St. Lawrence itself in Volume 19, from 1898. Thwaites turns the annual Relations toward Quebec and the Hurons under attack. The Iroquois strike at the heart of the French colony.

Sieges, raids, and captive-taking fill report after anxious report. Priests write through fear with their usual plain, direct style. Martyrs are made, and their deaths are told without flourish. The black robes serve as war reporters as much as pastors here. Their calm prose makes the terror of those years feel close and real. Duty holds firm even when safety is gone.
journal-of-discourses-vol-19:
John Taylor leads the church in Volume Nineteen, issued in 1878. The underground deepens as federal hunters press the Saints harder. Leaders hide, families scatter, and the kingdom stays defiant throughout.

Many discourses here were preached by men the marshals hunted daily. Sermons bless the hidden, stiffen the wavering, and damn the persecutors. Faith under real persecution speaks in its own hunted voice here. The price of the Saints' stand is counted in prison and exile. Readers meet devotion that paid in full for what it professed to believe. Taylor's calm command steadies a church learning to live underground.
treaty-of-versailles-1919:
The Treaty of Versailles, signed in 1919 in the palace's Hall of Mirrors, set the peace terms between the Allies and Germany after the First World War. Germany had no real part in drafting the terms and signed under protest. The treaty was one of several settlements that redrew the map of Europe after four years of slaughter.

Its articles placed sole blame for the war on Germany, demanded huge payments for war damage, and cut the German army to a small force. Germany lost land on its borders and all of its overseas colonies, and the League of Nations was created in the treaty's opening part. Many historians link the harsh terms to the anger that later fed the Second World War.
league-covenant-1919:
The Covenant of the League of Nations was adopted in 1919 as the first part of the Treaty of Versailles. It set up the world's first general body meant to keep peace between nations. President Woodrow Wilson championed the League, hoping that nations pledged to settle disputes by law would end the age of great wars.

The Covenant created an assembly and a council, promised aid to any member attacked, and laid out rules for cutting armaments and settling quarrels. Its weakness showed at once when the United States Senate refused to join. The League failed to stop the next world war, yet its structure and ideals passed directly into the United Nations.
say-traite-economie-politique-vol1-1819:
Say's Treatise on Political Economy reached its fourth French edition in 1819, and the first volume opens the work. Say was Adam Smith's great French interpreter, who recast the master's teaching into a clearer system. His Treatise became the most influential economics textbook of its age across Europe and America.

Volume 1 treats production: how wealth is created by industry, capital, and natural agents working together. Say gives the entrepreneur, the organizer who joins the factors and bears the risk, a central place that Smith had left vague. His famous law of markets, that supply creates its own demand, is stated in these chapters. The book taught Europe economics after Smith, in prose students could actually follow. The 1819 edition shows the system in its mature, author-revised form.
say-traite-economie-politique-vol2-1819:
Volume 2 of Say's Treatise, from the same 1819 fourth French edition, completes his system of political economy. The Treatise as a whole had already passed through many printings and translations, an honor no economics book of the age could match. Say revised each edition, and the fourth was his definitive statement.

The second volume carries the argument from production into distribution and consumption: how income is shared, and how wealth is used or wasted. Say treats public spending and taxation with the same wish for clarity that marks the first volume. The applied chapters show the doctrine meeting the facts of French economic life. Read with volume 1, the book gives the French master's full doctrine in its final form. It is the textbook that taught a generation, closed and complete.
veblen-place-of-science-1919:
Thorstein Veblen collected his essays as The Place of Science in Modern Civilisation in 1919. Veblen, the Norwegian-American economist who had coined the phrase conspicuous consumption, was the most original American social thinker of his age. The title essay asks why science flourishes in some ages and starves in others.

His answer credits idle curiosity, the disinterested wish to know, working against the practical and pecuniary habits of business culture. Other essays turn his irony on universities, which he treats as businesses in caps and gowns, and on the learned professions. Veblen's method is deadpan: he describes modern institutions as an anthropologist might describe a strange tribe. The volume shows him at his most characteristic. Readers who finish it tend to see their own institutions through his cold, amused eyes forever after.
veblen-vested-interests-1919:
Veblen published The Vested Interests and the Common Man in 1919, as the First World War ended and the peace was being made. The old iconoclast turned his irony into open anger for this short book. Its target is absentee ownership, the holding of industry by men who profit from it without working in it.

Veblen argues that owners keep prices high by holding back production, a kind of legal sabotage of the common good. Against them he sets the engineers and technicians who actually run the machines, and who might run them for use instead of profit. The book fed the brief vogue for technocracy that followed. It is Veblen's angriest work, written as the world remade itself and he hoped, in vain, for a different peace. The prophet of the engineers' republic speaks here without his usual smile.
weimar-constitution-1919:
Germany's National Assembly adopted the Weimar Constitution in 1919, meeting in the town of Weimar because Berlin was in turmoil. The empire had collapsed in defeat and revolution, and the assembly had to found a republic on the ruins. Hugo Preuss drafted much of the text, aiming at the most democratic law of its day.

The charter gives the vote to all adults, women included, with seats shared by proportion of votes. It promises a full list of basic rights, from free speech to welfare duties of the state. It also arms the president with emergency powers, later used to rule by decree. The republic it founded lived only fourteen years before Hitler destroyed it. The noblest and most ill-fated founding law of modern Europe still teaches how democracies die.
us-amendment-19:
Women gained a clear shield for the ballot when the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. Congress had passed it in 1919, after a long campaign by suffrage groups across the country. The amendment says the right to vote cannot be denied because of sex.

Its single sentence doubled the pool of people who could take part in elections. Women had won the vote in some states earlier, but now the rule held nationwide. The change closed a fight that had lasted more than seventy years. It still stands as a landmark step toward equal citizenship in the United States.
cia-0000010919:
Ferdinand Marcos had just taken office as president of the Philippines when the CIA weighed the country's prospects in January 1966. The paper covers internal security along with foreign and domestic problems. The Philippines was an American ally sending troops to Vietnam, yet it still faced unrest at home left over from the old Huk rebellion.

Analysts looked at Marcos's early grip on power and the restless politics of the islands. They weighed the fading Huk movement and the strains on the economy and government. Read later, the estimate stands near the start of a rule that would end in martial law and dictatorship.
cia-0000012419:
The fortieth debriefing: meeting number forty falls on October 10, 1961, in the Paris phase. The number itself testifies to the operation's scale and stamina over two seasons. Forty sessions in under six months, across three cities, with one source giving everything he knew. No Western intelligence operation had ever debriefed a source so thoroughly, and the file's plain numbering makes the record without any need for boasting.

The record marks the milestone in the series' usual plain form. Handlers by then could measure the colonel's whole knowledge in sittings. For readers, the page is the count made visible: forty, and still the questions came.
cia-0000013219:
Take them alive: Viet Cong instructions stressing the capture of American personnel fill a CIA item from April 1971. Living prisoners were worth more than dead enemies. They could be questioned, traded, and shown to the cameras. The take-alive guidance shaped how patrols acted on both sides. Men who knew the other side wanted prisoners fought with that knowledge in mind during every ambush.

The item preserves the other side's playbook in its own terms. Such instructions explained patterns American units had noticed the hard way. For readers, it is a tactical page with a human edge: the value set on a living enemy.
cia-0000014619: Travel to Mexico by the family of Morton Sobell is tracked in a CIA file dated June 2, 1958. Sobell was serving a long prison term for his part in the Rosenberg spy case. His family's trips abroad drew official watch for years after the trial. The file is one piece of the long tail of surveillance that followed that case.
cia-0000014719: Letters concerning Julius and Ethel Rosenberg fill a CIA file dated February 2, 1954. The file came months after the couple's execution in June 1953. Letters about them kept arriving at offices long after their deaths. Gathering them shows how the case lived on as a cause, argued in mailbags as much as in courts.
cia-0000015319: A letter to Donald Keyhoe from J. S. Harman fills a CIA file dated September 5, 1958. Harman thanks Keyhoe for his letter of September 22, dates again reversed in the title. Keyhoe's charges of a cover up never slowed. The agency's calm, short replies never changed either, year after year. This Keyhoe letter is now kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015419: Student papers on flying saucers, sent in by Dr. Thornton Page, reached the CIA in a file dated January 2, 1960. Page was an astronomer who had served on the government's early saucer panel. That students were writing class papers on the subject shows how far it had spread. The agency kept the papers, one more sign that saucers had entered campus life.
cia-0000022219: American casualties in Son La Province, North Vietnam, are recorded in a CIA item dated in 1974. Son La is a mountain province in the northwest of the country. By 1974 the last American combat troops had left Vietnam, yet the counting of the lost went on. A province level tally served the long work of accounting for every man.
cia-0000022319: Moscow would let two Virginia lawyers represent Gary Powers, a CIA record dated August 4, 1985, reports in its heading. Even so, the heading keeps a real step in the famous case.
cia-0000022619: Three American prisoners of war were sighted in southern Laos in mid June 1971, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. Southern Laos held the Ho Chi Minh Trail country, where many airmen fell. A mid June date fixes the sighting in the wet season of that year. The report joined the stack of leads checked against the missing lists.
cia-0000036519:

The estimate looks at the likely fallout across Africa and beyond if the declaration went ahead. It weighs unrest, diplomacy, and the strain on Britain and its allies. Forecasts like this let readers see a crisis as officials saw it, before the outcome was known. Rhodesia did in fact declare independence alone later that same year, in November.

Inside, the reported admission is recorded as it reached the file. Owning the seizure changed the talks at a stroke if true. It told the government exactly whose terms it had to meet. Until then, even the authorship of the seizure had been part of what the talks had to settle. The record preserves the claim and its hedge together, which is honest history: the admission as reported, with the doubt of the first reporting still attached.

plos-pone-0005719: Hawkmoths lack a strong family tree. Kawahara and team built a family tree from five nuclear genes. The framework supports varied biological studies. Moths' map, drawn from DNA, 1400 species placed in context, lepidopteran biogeography clarified, a model group finally mapped.

plos-pone-0006419: Plant bits guard bone blood flow. Zhang and team found Epimedium flavonoids cut steroid-linked bone death in a dose-wise way. The guard works through blood, not bone — herbs versus bone rot, tested, fixing two blood faults. Clots and fat buildup.
plos-pone-0006519: A cell guard shapes lung defense. Prakash and team found cIAP-1 steers innate immunity to Chlamydophila pneumoniae lung attack. plos-pone-0006619: Yeast genes that shrug off caffeine. Calvo and team screened fission yeast for caffeine-tolerance genes. The survivors' secrets, mapped — coffee's tiny testers, mapped, past cell-killing excess. Schizosaccharomyces pombe, oxygen stress link: mutants hunted, growth stalled, shrug-off's genes, complex cells all hit.
plos-pone-0009419: Great apes are hard to watch in dense forest, so scientists read their droppings for clues — and found vertebrate DNA in bonobo and gorilla dung. The puzzle: did these supposed plant-eaters eat meat, or is the DNA contamination? The paper weighs the evidence for both, showing how a fecal sample can either rewrite ape diets or warn researchers about lab artifacts.
plos-pone-0009519: Clover-like legumes team up with soil bacteria to make nitrogen fertilizer from thin air, building root nodules as shared factories. plos-pone-0009619: Biologists read papers through their figures — so why do search engines ignore them? This study tests BioText, a search engine that indexes full text plus figures and captions. The paper shows that figure-aware search finds what text-only search misses.
plos-pone-0010419: Did farming spread through Europe by migrating farmers or by neighbors copying the idea? Comparing Y-chromosome DNA in Sardinia and Anatolia, this study favors cultural diffusion. plos-pone-0010519: Fruit flies manage magnesium with a single TRPM channel — unlike humans with eight. This study shows the fly channel is essential for extracellular magnesium control. plos-pone-0010619: Tomorrow's factories might be vats of teamed-up germs. This study builds a mock community of microbes that reacts to its surroundings as one unit. plos-pone-0010719: Sendai virus dodges the immune system with its C protein. This study shows conserved charged amino acids play multiple roles in that evasion. The paper dissects a viral trick. The molecular detail informs paramyxovirus biology and guides future antiviral research efforts.
plos-pone-0010819: When cells fail to split, cancer can follow. This study shows a c-Myc target protein links cytokinesis failure to oncogenic signaling in human cells.
